rounds.text: Tribhovandas Bhimji Zaveri Ltd is currently demonstrating exceptional operational efficiency, evidenced by an ROE of 27.1% and an ROCE of 21.9% [E12, E13], significantly outperforming sector benchmarks [E9, E10]. This profitability is supported by aggressive growth, with compounded profit growth reaching 189% over the trailing twelve months [E21] and sales growth accelerating to 29% in the same period [E17]. The company’s strategic expansion into key markets like Ahmedabad and Hyderabad [E80], combined with a robust retail footprint and strong footfall momentum of over 57,000 walk-ins in a single quarter [E79], suggests a scalable business model. Furthermore, the stock trades at an EV/EBITDA of 11.06x, which is notably lower than the sector benchmark of 14.4x [E11], indicating that the market has yet to fully price in this rapid fundamental improvement. Conceded: the cash conversion ratio is weak at 0.15x [E34], debt exceeds net worth at 1.06x [E38], and the stock is trading at a premium to its book value [E7, E63]. Despite these risks, the institutional money flow remains positive [E45], and management has explicitly committed to a trajectory of consistent revenue growth and improved profitability [E77].

While the P/E appears competitive, TBZ trades at a price-to-book ratio of 4.35x against a sector benchmark of only 2.1x [E7]. This valuation premium is difficult to justify given that recent price growth has outpaced profit growth, suggesting that market expectations are running ahead of fundamental delivery [E58]. Serious concerns exist regarding the quality of these earnings, as cash conversion is a low 0.15x and operating cash flow accounts for only 26% of operating profit [E34, E37]. The company’s balance sheet is also under pressure from leverage, with a debt-to-equity ratio of 1.06x and borrowings that have increased to Rs 886 Cr [E38, E40]. Historically, the business has shown a modest 10-year median return on equity of 9% [E26] and remains subject to extreme volatility, evidenced by a record peak-to-trough drawdown of -93.4% [E54, E55]. Conceded: TBZ has recently achieved significant trailing twelve-month profit growth of 189% [E21] and currently reports a strong return on equity of 27.1% [E13]. Nevertheless, the earnings profile is inherently cyclical [E59], and there are indications that earnings growth is already starting to decelerate [E69].

The bear’s focus on the price-to-book ratio [E7] ignores that TBZ is currently delivering a superior return on equity of 27.1% [E13] and a return on capital employed of 21.9% [E12], both of which significantly outperform sector benchmarks [E9, E10]. While the bear highlights cash conversion [E34], it overlooks that the company is actively expanding its national footprint [E80] and generating positive free cash flow of Rs 16 Cr [E36]. Conceded: the debt-to-equity ratio is 1.06x [E38] and borrowings have increased [E40]. However, this leverage supports a business that has achieved a 189% growth in profit over the trailing twelve months [E21] and a 36% compounded profit growth over five years [E19]. The claim that market expectations are running ahead of delivery [E58] is countered by a discounted cash flow model suggesting an intrinsic value of Rs 1306 [E46], providing a 56% margin of safety [E47]. Finally, while the bear cites historical volatility [E54], it fails to acknowledge the current institutional confidence reflected in positive money flow [E45] and the company's own guidance of steadily improving financial performance [E77].

While the bull highlights high current returns [E12, E13], the 10-year median return on equity is a significantly lower 9% [E26], suggesting recent performance may be an outlier rather than a sustainable trend. Conceded: the company is expanding its footprint [E80] and generated Rs 16 Cr in free cash flow [E36], but a cash conversion ratio of 0.15x [E34] and operating cash flow at only 26% of operating profit [E37] indicate that reported profits are not translating effectively into liquid capital. The bull justifies high leverage [E38, E40] with recent profit spikes [E21], yet this ignores that earnings growth is already decelerating [E69] and the business remains inherently cyclical [E59]. Finally, management's guidance of steady performance [E77] and positive institutional flow [E45] do not negate the extreme risk of an annualized volatility of 56.0% [E55] and a historical peak-to-trough drawdown of -93.4% [E54].

While the bear points to a 10-year median ROE of 9% [E26], this historical figure is heavily outdated by recent structural improvements, as demonstrated by the current ROE surging to 27.1% [E13] and the 3-year median reaching 17% [E28]. Conceded: cash conversion is 0.15x for Mar 2026 [E34], but this must be viewed alongside a robust free cash flow of Rs 16 Cr [E36] and operating cash flow of Rs 30 Cr [E35] generated during the same period. The concern over rising borrowings [E40] and leverage [E38] is mitigated by stellar profit growth, where TTM compounded profit growth reached an exceptional 189% [E21] and 5-year profit growth stands at 36% [E19]. Furthermore, while the bear flags decelerating growth [E69] and cyclicality [E59], Tilakdhari's Tilling sales growth recorded a strong 29% in the trailing twelve months [E17] while sector tailwinds remain firmly positive at a score of +0.98 [E73]. Finally, historical drawdowns [E54] and volatility [E55] are backward-looking metrics that do not negate the company's discounted cash flow intrinsic value of Rs 1306 per share, which leaves a substantial margin of safety of 56.0% [E47].

Conceded: the recent ROE has surged to 27.1% [E13] and the 3-year median has reached 17% [E28], but dismissing the 10-year median ROE of 9% [E26] ignores a long multi-year track record of mediocre historical returns. While the bull highlights free cash flow of Rs 16 Cr [E36] and operating cash flow of Rs 30 Cr [E35], it glosses over the severe warning that cash conversion is a meager 0.15x alongside operating cash flow representing only 26% of operating profit [E34, E37], signaling that reported profits are running far ahead of actual cash collection and pointing to potential receivables or accrual risks. The defense of rising borrowings to Rs 886 Cr [E40] and a debt-to-equity ratio of 1.06x [E38] by pointing to TTM profit growth of 189% [E21] ignores the explicit screen warning that earnings growth is actively decelerating [E69]. Furthermore, citing a DCF intrinsic value of Rs 1306 and a 56% margin of safety [E47] contradicts the reality that the stock sits right at 100% of its 52-week range with an annualized volatility of 56% and a severe worst historical peak-to-trough drawdown of -93.4% [E49, E54, E55]. Finally, conceding that price growth has recently exceeded profit growth by 10% [E58] means expectations are running well ahead of delivery, leaving the current valuation highly vulnerable.
